To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) age-related decreases in pol alpha expression, activity and fidelity in HDF, as measured by in vitro DNA synthesis, and in murine liver, as measured by both in vivo and in vitro DNA synthesis; (2) dietary restriction impedes the decline in both specific activity and fidelity in hepatic pol alpha; and (3). pol alpha expression and activity in HDF are increased by transformation.

(1) DNA polymerase alpha from human fibroblasts and from mouse livers shows age-related declines in mRNA levels and enzyme activity; (2) dietary restriction (DR) retards the decline in enzyme specific activity in the mouse liver; (3) pol alpha from transformed cells is more active than from normal cells and is expressed at higher levels in the normal cells; and (4) the accessory protein for pol alpha may interact with the polymerase differently in young and aged cells.

age-related changes in DNA polymerase alpha activity, expression and fidelity are associated with decreased DNA binding of the enzyme, and that the age-related decrease in DNA binding can be partially overcome by treatment of the enzyme with a DNA polymerase alpha accessory protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the age-related changes in the expression, specific activity and fidelity, of DNA polymerase in both HDF and murine hepatic cells and tissues, as well as with the effect of dietary restriction on the age-related changes.

the effects of aging and dietary restriction on expression, activity, and fidelity of DNA polymerase, and on the interactions of DNA polymerase with accessory proteins, in normal and transformed human and murine cells.
the role of pol alpha in the maintenance of genome stability in mammalian cells and tissues, with particular emphasis on the effects of aging, dietary restriction, and cellular transformation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the absence of a dietary restriction regimen, there is a progressive decline in the specific activity of pol alpha as a function of aging in HDF and murine hepatic tissue.

the decline in specific activity of pol alpha with increasing age is not due to an intrinsic change in the enzyme itself, but is likely due to a change in the enzyme's interaction with an accessory protein.

the age-related changes in pol alpha expression, specific activity and fidelity are complex and multifactorial, and that dietary restriction can alter the age-related changes of pol alpha in a positive way.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

age-related changes in DNA replication are due, at least in part, to changes in the expression and activity of pol alpha, that dietary restriction impedes age-related declines in pol alpha activity and fidelity in mice, and that pol alpha accessory proteins may play a role in age-related changes in pol alpha activity.

the age-associated decline in the expression and activity of pol alpha in HDF, and the age- associated decline in the specific activity and fidelity in hepatic tissues, is not a universal phenomenon, but rather is dependent upon the cell/tissue type and the nutritional environment.
the age-related decline in DNA polymerase alpha expression and activity in both HDF and mouse livers is a function of the loss of an essential pol alpha accessory protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expression of pol alpha in human cells is age dependent.
the fidelity and activity of pol alpha is decreased with increasing age in human cells and in essentially amitotically dividing murine hepatic cells.
the decline in polalpha expression and activity in HDF and in pol alpha fidelity in murine hepatic tissue with age is a function of the decline in pol-alpha expression.
